one_liner: Linux-kernel TLS 1.2 server stack in the Tempesta FW proxy; 6-83% more handshakes/s than Nginx+OpenSSL in vendor tests.
what_it_does: Tempesta TLS is the TLS layer of Tempesta FW, an HTTPS reverse proxy, web accelerator and WAF that runs as an out-of-tree kernel module on a patched Linux kernel. It terminates server-side TLS 1.2 inside the kernel's TCP/IP stack, so TCP and TLS handshakes both finish before any user-space process is involved. It is not a library with an OpenSSL-like API: you adopt it by replacing Nginx/HAProxy TLS termination with Tempesta FW and configuring it through Tempesta's own config file. It began as a fork of mbed TLS 2.8.0, but the README says only the PKI interface code from mbed TLS remains.
how_it_is_fast: The handshake runs in SoftIRQ right after the TCP handshake, with a zero-copy state machine on skbs, so there are no user/kernel context switches, socket syscalls or extra copies. Hot paths make no heap allocations: each cipher suite has a precomputed 'MPI profile' that is copied in one shot, and temporary big integers come from per-CPU page pools. P-256 uses hand-written x86-64 BMI2/ADX Montgomery arithmetic (after Gueron-Krasnov) in Jacobian coordinates, with fixed-base comb tables (window 7) for m*G, RDRAND randomization in place of full constant-time table scans, and the Linux crypto API for AES-GCM/CCM. The paper reports 40x the original mbed TLS port's rate (2,180 vs 51 handshakes/s), but raw ECDSA/ECDHE op/s stay below OpenSSL's, so the gain over Nginx comes from where the code runs, not from faster math.
when_to_use: Dedicated x86-64 Linux edge servers where full or resumed TLS handshakes/s is the bottleneck, for example short-lived HTTPS connections or TLS handshake floods (DDoS), and you can replace Nginx/HAProxy with Tempesta FW
Traffic dominated by session resumption through RFC 5077 session tickets: the paper measured 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%) against Nginx/OpenSSL on bare metal
Small VMs without virtual APIC, where fewer VM exits matter: on a 1-vCPU KVM guest, the paper measured +41% handshakes/s and 77% lower average latency
ECDSA P-256 certificates with ECDHE P-256 and AES-GCM suites, serving HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (the only ALPN protocols supported)
Deployments that want private and session keys held in non-swappable kernel memory, away from the application's address space
when_not_to_use: You need TLS 1.3, X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, P-384 or client-side TLS: only TLS 1.2 server-side with AES-GCM/CCM on secp256r1 is supported, and TLS 1.3 (issue #1031) is still open
You need a library to link into your own application or into Nginx/HAProxy: there is no OpenSSL-compatible API, and the kernel TLS socket API (issue #1433) is only a proposal

Bare-metal services that care about tail latency: in the paper, Nginx/OpenSSL had 50-170% lower average and p95 latency for new sessions, and Tempesta's max latency was up to 30x worse (28,262 vs 925 ms) under load

Non-x86-64 hardware (ARM/Graviton), CPUs without BMI2/ADX, or managed kernels: the product needs a patched kernel (linux-6.12.12-tfw for 0.9/master, 5.10.35-tfw for 0.8), at least 8 GB RAM, 2 MB huge pages and an RSS-capable NIC
RSA-certificate workloads (the docs say RSA isn't performance-optimized), or teams that cannot accept a Beta, GPLv2 in-kernel TLS stack that enlarges the kernel TCB

integration.dependencies: Patched Linux kernel (tempesta-tech/linux-6.12.12-tfw for 0.9/master, linux-5.10.35-tfw for release-0.8); Linux crypto API for symmetric ciphers and hashes; build packages listed in the install docs include gcc, g++, libboost-all-dev, libssl-dev, libelf-dev, flex, bison and dwarves
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (no GCC version given); Ubuntu 24.04 is the preferred build and run environment; needs kernel headers and 35-40 GB of disk for the kernel build
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux only; SSE4.2, BMI2 and ADX are required by the Makefile. AVX2 is listed as required in the docs, and the Makefile warns not to use builds without it in production. Needs RDRAND and huge-page support.
integration.thread_safety: Kernel-internal: handshake steps run in non-preemptible SoftIRQ on per-CPU MPI pools, and each connection's TLS context is guarded by a spinlock (tls->lock). There is no public user-space API.

gotchas: Side-channel protection mixes constant-time code with non-constant-time code plus RDRAND randomization (as in mbed TLS) rather than OpenSSL's constant-time-everywhere approach. A CRYPTO_CONST_TIME build flag exists. On SRBDS-affected Intel CPUs, the microcode mitigation cuts RDRAND to about 3% of its original speed, and the requirements page says the mitigation is needed in public clouds.
Curve25519 source (tls/ec_25519.c) is present but marked 'slow and incomplete' and is not in the supported-curve list; secp256r1 is the only ECDHE curve offered.
Heavy public-key math runs in SoftIRQ with kernel_fpu_begin/end. The paper links this to tail-latency spikes and packet drops under heavy load on bare metal.
The master branch is a development (unstable) branch. The README says to use release-0.8 for a stable version, and the project calls itself Beta.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: AWS-LC and wolfSSL are user-space libraries that link into HAProxy or Nginx, support TLS 1.3 and ARM, and scale across many cores (their benchmarks use a 64-core Graviton4). Pick Tempesta only when you can replace the whole HTTPS proxy on dedicated x86-64 Linux and TLS 1.2 ECDSA-P-256 handshake cost per core is your limit, since its gain comes from kernel placement and its own crypto is slower than OpenSSL's.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' NetDev 0x14 (2020) paper ran TLS 1.2 ECDHE-ECDSA P-256 handshakes against Tempesta FW on Linux 5.7 and Nginx 1.19.1 + OpenSSL 1.1.1d, using tls-perf and wrk; on a 1-vCPU KVM guest (i7-6500U host, no vAPIC), Tempesta reached 2,180 vs 1,545 handshakes/s with 307 vs 1,340 ms average latency. On bare-metal Xeon E3-1240v5 limited to one physical core (2 hyperthreads) with 10GbE, it gained 83% on resumption but only 6% on new sessions (7,921 vs 7,426), with worse average, p95 and max latency; compiler and build flags are not given.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-25; Ubuntu 24 package release 0.8.2 in October 2025) but still self-described Beta; GPL-2.0 kernel module deployed as a complete reverse proxy, not a TLS library you can vendor into another program.
